acbl17:388: Jason Wei’s insight—“the ease with which you can improve a system is proportional to how easily you can verify its outputs”—has special meaning in the field of Agent reliability. Traditional software systems have clear correctness criteria (unit tests, integration tests). The challenge of Agent systems is that judgment-type outputs (“Is this answer useful?”) have no ground truth, so they cannot be verified with traditional tests. Skillify’s multi-layer verification system answers this: deterministic functions are verified with unit tests, real data with integration tests, judgment quality with LLM-as-judge, routing logic with resolver eval, and end-to-end with smoke tests. Every failure mode has a corresponding test layer, none are overlooked. The deeper implication of this design is: when you can independently and repeatedly verify each capability of an Agent, improvement becomes an engineering problem—you can measure, locate, fix, and re-measure. You go from “it feels like the Agent has gotten better” to “this metric improved from X% to Y%.”

hatebg:321: This loop works because it resolves a fundamental contradiction: the Agent’s reasoning ability is both the source of reliability problems and the solution to them. If you simply let the Agent work on “vibes,” it will reason on its own where certainty is required (making Type I errors); if you over-constrain the Agent, it loses the ability to use judgment to handle new problems. Skillify’s bootstrap loop lets the model decide for itself “where certainty is needed,” then solidifies that decision into structural constraints. This means the system does not rely on prompts to “tell” the Agent when to reason and when to use scripts—rather, the Agent uses its reasoning ability to write the judgment criteria itself, and then uses those criteria to constrain itself.
